chapter_theme: Songs at Tiruvakkarai (திருவக்கரை): the poet asks to stop babbling scriptures without speaking of Murugan, to escape the hell the womb leads to and the round of births, and to be counted among his servants; and asks to be freed from courtesans who paint their faces and grasp at money while the world says 'shame'.

722.reading: The poet asks that he stop babbling some scriptures noisily without saying even a little about Murugan, not fall again and again into the cruel hell the path of the womb leads to, and stop wandering through many births in the world, and that he, a dog of a servant, be taken into the throng of Murugan's servants and given the two flower feet. The praise names the peacock hero who fought the night-roamer until the great mountains cracked and the sea dried, the hunter girl's lover, the lord of Tiruvakkarai where conches crawl in the waves and give up pearls, who grants devotees whatever they wish.
722.nuance: கலைகள் பிதற்றுவது: learning recited without the Lord is the first thing the poet wants to give up, before hell and rebirth. உனதடிமைத் திரள் அதனினும் உட்பட: the plea is to belong to the company of servants, not only to reach the feet alone.

723.reading: The poet describes the women who rub green herbs on their faces to make them shine, cunning in crafty arts, who think only of seizing the money in a man's hand, who bewitch with pearl smiles and glances, give the spittle of their lips as if fruit and sugar, flatter on the cushioned bed and draw him into their embrace; he asks for the good feet so that he may give up this trade and this habit, which leave him wretched every day while the world says 'chi, chi'. The praise names Vishnu who sleeps on the serpent, Lakshmi's lord with the conch and tulasi, who set the mountain in the sea and churned out nectar, as uncle, Murugan dear to the hunter girl of rustic speech, and the lord of Tiruvakkarai of lotus fields and moat.
723.nuance: உலகத்தவர் சிச்சியெனத் திரி: public contempt is part of the poet's suffering. இத்தொழில் இக்குணம்: he calls his own habit a trade, as if visiting courtesans were his occupation.

links.note: Both see the courtesan's sweetness as aimed at a man's money: the Kural warns that such women's sweet words bring harm, and 723 shows the flattery on the bed with the hand already reaching for the purse.

722 begins by asking to stop babbling scriptures noisily (கலகலெனச் சில கலைகள் பிதற்றுவது) without saying even a little about Murugan. Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the pure one's feet (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல்). Both judge learning by whether it turns to the Lord; the song makes it the first thing to renounce, before hell and rebirth.

723 counts among its sufferings that the world says 'chi, chi' (உலகத்தவர் சிச்சியெனத் திரி) at the man who trades in courtesans. Naladiyar 377 says those who think a courtesan's love their own, while she takes the wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). Both name public contempt, not only lost money, as the price.
